integrated product and service portfolio to meet the evolving needs of Bangladesh’s Ready-Made

PREFACE
This report presents the 10-year financial strategy and expansion roadmap for Milliner Wears
Accessories Limited, a well-established name in Bangladesh’s garments accessories
manufacturing sector. Recognizing the dynamic growth of the country’s Ready-Made Garments

strengthen its competitive positioning in both domestic and international markets.

reliability and quality. In response to rising global demand and the sustained expansion of
Bangladesh’s RMG exports—marked by a 10.33% year-on-year increase in FY 2023–24 as
reported by the Export Promotion Bureau (EPB)—the company has developed a comprehensive
financial and investment plan that will guide its transition into a large-scale, vertically integrated
manufacturing hub.

Industry Risk Analysis
The risk analysis of garment accessories sector of Bangladesh covers Porter’s five factors model.
Besides, we also consider other externalities including changes in Govt. regulations, technological
adaptation, productivity, infrastructural development etc. to understand the overall industry
attractiveness. The industry risk characteristics of the garment accessories sector are described
briefly as follows:
Bargaining Power of Suppliers
The suppliers' negotiating influence in the garment accessories sector tends to range from low to
moderate. This is attributed to the abundance of suppliers for raw materials such as fabrics and
threads, with the notable presence of numerous small and medium-sized suppliers within
industry. However, in cases where certain materials have limited suppliers, those specific
suppliers may exert more significant bargaining power.
Bargaining Power of Buyers
Buyers (i.e., international retailers) in the garment accessories sector typically have moderate to
high bargaining power. This is because there are numerous producers in the market, giving
buyers a lot of choices. Moreover, the standardization of products in the industry enables buyers
to seamlessly switch between suppliers, considering factors such as price, quality, and other
relevant considerations.
Threat of New Entrants
The garment accessories industry requires a significant amount of capital for setting up factories
and establishing supply chains. However, the relative ease of replicating production processes
and the availability of cheap workforces in Bangladesh may attract new entrants. Government
policies and regulations also play a role in determining ease of entry. Hence, there is a moderate
threat of new entrants.
Threat of Substitutes
The threat of substitutes is relatively low, as there are limited alternatives to clothing and apparel.
However, changes in consumer preferences, such as a shift towards sustainable or alternative
materials, could increase the threat of substitutes. The industry's ability to adapt to changing
trends and preferences will influence this force.

Strategic Investment Plan and Financing Pattern:
Milliner Wears Accessories Limited has strategically developed a comprehensive and vertically
integrated product and service portfolio to meet the evolving needs of Bangladesh’s Ready-Made
Garments (RMG) sector. Currently, the company manufactures key garment accessories including
elastic bands, narrow fabrics, drawstrings, and both plastic and metal tipping. As part of its
forward-looking expansion plan, the company aims to diversify and scale its offerings in a phased
approach. In Phase 1, the product line will expand to include twill tape, sewing threads, printed
and woven labels, screen and offset printing services, poly bags, hangers, and gum tape. Phase
2 will introduce interlining, pocketing fabrics, buttons, zippers, and multi-ply carton boxes—
further strengthening the company’s backward linkage capabilities. In Phase 3, Milliner Wears
will enter into value-added services such as fabric dyeing, yarn dyeing, and establishing a full-
scale washing plant. Upon full implementation of all three phases, the company will operate 26
interrelated product lines, transforming into a one-stop solution provider for garment accessories.
This integrated portfolio will enhance operational synergy, increase customer retention, and
solidify Milliner Wears’ position as a leading player in the garments accessories industry.
The fixed cost of the project across all phases is estimated at USD 34.42 million, entirely financed
through equity contributions. The initial setup involved USD 985,000, while Phase 1 and Phase 2
require USD 4.42 million and USD 6.84 million respectively, with the largest share of USD 22.17
million allocated to Phase 3 for establishing the dyeing and washing facilities.

the investment period. Unlike fixed assets, working capital requirements will be financed using a
mix of debt and equity. The current working capital of USD 1.04 million is funded with a 43%
debt and 57% equity mix. Future working capital needs will rise significantly: USD 6.4 million in

Milliner Wears Accessories Limited
Investment in Phase: 3
Phase 3 of Milliner Wears Accessories Limited’s expansion, scheduled for Year 5, marks the
company’s most ambitious investment yet, with a total planned outlay of USD 30 million. This
phase focuses on backward integration and technological sophistication, particularly through the
establishment of a comprehensive dyeing and washing facility, supported by environmental
compliance systems like a biological ETP (Effluent Treatment Plant). The fixed cost of the project
totals USD 22.17 million, with the remaining USD 7.83 million allocated to working capital,
ensuring the smooth operation of the expanded infrastructure.
A significant component of this phase is the USD 14.16 million investment in imported dyeing
and washing machinery, reflecting a strategic shift toward vertical integration to enhance
production control, quality assurance, and sustainability. Infrastructure development is robust,
with USD 4.36 million allocated to civil construction, which includes 97,500 sq. ft. of production
floor, 7,500 sq. ft. of bonded warehouse, and additional utility and security structures. Land
development costs total USD 1.48 million for 100 decimals, acquired at a higher rate of USD
12,774.11 per decimal, indicative of increased land value and the premium nature of the site.
Additional investments include utility setup (USD 491,803) for a 2000 KVA substation,
generators, and compressors, while furniture, vehicles, and pre-operating expenses collectively
represent close to USD 1.36 million. Notably, USD 983,607 has been designated for a logistics
fleet, including 5 trucks, 5 medium covered vans, and 5 private cars, underscoring the company’s
focus on internal logistics efficiency.
With this phase, Milliner Wears positions itself as a vertically integrated, environmentally
responsible, and high-capacity player in the garment accessories industry. The integration of
dyeing and washing capabilities will drastically reduce dependency on external processors,
improve lead times, and support large-scale export readiness, all while enhancing compliance
with global environmental and safety standards. Phase 3 represents not just expansion, but
transformation—equipping the company for long-term global competitiveness and operational
excellence.

Investor Earnings Dividend Sharing Plan and Exit Strategy:
Investment Phases
• Phase 1 (Year 1): $8 million for expanding current production and setting up a new product
line.
• Phase 2 (Year 3): $12 million for upgrading production lines + establishing printing &
packaging.
• Phase 3 (Year 5): $30 million for dyeing and washing facility setup.
Dividend sharing plan:
The dividend policy will follow a structured and sustainable approach aligned with the company’s
growth and reinvestment needs over the 10-year horizon. In the short term (Years 2 to 3), the
company will adopt a conservative dividend payout strategy, targeting approximately 10% of net
profit to be distributed as dividends, allowing sufficient retention for working capital and capacity
expansion under Phase 1 and Phase 2 of the investment.
During the mid-term period (Years 4 to 6), as the business stabilizes and begins generating
stronger cash flow from expanded and upgraded facilities, the dividend payout ratio will increase
to around 30% of net profit. This phase balances investor returns with continued reinvestment,
particularly for the dyeing and washing facility setup.
In the long term (Years 7 to 10), once the full benefits of vertical integration and scale efficiencies
are realized, the company will target a dividend payout of up to 40% of net profit, providing
attractive and consistent returns to equity investors while still maintaining reserves for
operational resilience and strategic opportunities.
The investor’s share of dividends will be proportionate to their equity stake in the company, with
distributions made annually or semi-annually, subject to board approval and cash flow
availability.
Exit Strategy
The exit strategy for the foreign investor is designed to provide both flexibility and value
maximization, aligned with the company’s phased growth trajectory. In the short term (Years 1
to 3), the investor will be subject to a lock-in period to ensure stability and commitment during
the initial expansion phase. During this time, exit options will be limited, although exceptional
situations—such as strategic misalignment or material financial risk—may allow for a negotiated
partial exit. Any such exit would be based on book value or a mutually agreed internal rate of
return to protect the interests of both parties.
